claim: Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) fail to infect neurons in the zebrafish brain.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), which are widely used for gene transfer in mammals and other amniotes, fail to infect neurons in the zebrafish brain (Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2009

claim: HSV1 can infect zebrafish neurons both locally and retrogradely via projecting axons without obvious signs of cytotoxicity.
source: We first focused on herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1), a DNA virus that can infect zebrafish neurons both locally and retrogradely via projecting axons without obvious signs of cytotoxicity (Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2014

claim: Zebrafish are usually kept at 26–28.5 °C in the laboratory.
source: Zebrafish are usually kept at 26–28.5 °C but the temperature range of natural habitats is broad (up to >38 °C) and temperature tolerance in the laboratory extends up to ~41 °C (Engeszer et al., 2007; López-Olmeda and Sánchez-Vázquez, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engeszer et al., 2007 and López-Olmeda and Sánchez-Vázquez, 2011

claim: The temperature range of zebrafish natural habitats is broad, up to >38 °C.
source: Zebrafish are usually kept at 26–28.5 °C but the temperature range of natural habitats is broad (up to >38 °C) and temperature tolerance in the laboratory extends up to ~41 °C (Engeszer et al., 2007; López-Olmeda and Sánchez-Vázquez, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engeszer et al., 2007 and López-Olmeda and Sánchez-Vázquez, 2011

claim: Temperature tolerance of zebrafish in the laboratory extends up to ~41 °C.
source: Zebrafish are usually kept at 26–28.5 °C but the temperature range of natural habitats is broad (up to >38 °C) and temperature tolerance in the laboratory extends up to ~41 °C (Engeszer et al., 2007; López-Olmeda and Sánchez-Vázquez, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engeszer et al., 2007 and López-Olmeda and Sánchez-Vázquez, 2011

claim: Survival rates of adult zebrafish were 100% for 10 days post injection in all treatment groups, independent of temperature.
source: In adult fish, survival rates were 100% for 10 days post injection in all treatment groups, independent of temperature (N=5 fish per treatment group; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In larvae, survival during the first three days after injection was always >90%.
source: In larvae, some mortality occurred in all groups, which is likely to be natural. Mortality was slightly enhanced at elevated temperatures but survival during the first three days, which are most relevant for viral gene transfer (see below), was always >90% (N=30 fish per group; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: At 36 °C, the mean swimming speed of adult fish was increased compared to 26 °C.
source: At 36 °C, the mean swimming speed of adult fish was increased and fish stayed, on average, slightly higher in the water column than at 26 °C (Speed: p<0.001, Z position: p<0.001; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001)

claim: At 36 °C, fish stayed, on average, slightly higher in the water column than at 26 °C.
source: At 36 °C, the mean swimming speed of adult fish was increased and fish stayed, on average, slightly higher in the water column than at 26 °C (Speed: p<0.001, Z position: p<0.001; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001)

claim: Social distance was not significantly different between fish at 36 °C and 26 °C.
source: However, the general swimming pattern appeared similar (Figure 1—videos 1–4) and social distance was not significantly different (p=0.53, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p=0.53) and visual data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: No significant effects on swimming speed were observed when fish were returned to standard laboratory temperatures after seven days at 36 °C.
source: No significant effects on swimming speed were observed when fish were returned to standard laboratory temperatures after seven days at 36 °C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: Learning in an odor discrimination task was not significantly different between control fish and fish injected with HSV1 and kept at 36 °C for 2 days.
source: Learning was assessed by a standard discrimination score and not significantly different between groups (p=0.76; Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p=0.76) and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Swimming behavior and olfactory discrimination learning were not significantly impaired by virus injection with subsequent incubation at temperatures near 37 °C.
source: These results confirm that swimming behavior and olfactory discrimination learning were not significantly impaired by virus injection with subsequent incubation at temperatures near 37 °C.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on swimming behavior and learning

claim: Reporter expression (DsRed) was observed in the injected olfactory bulb after HSV1[LTCMV:DsRed] injection.
source: Consistent with previous results (Zou et al., 2014), reporter expression (DsRed) was observed in the injected OB.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2014 and experimental observation

claim: Retrogradely labeled neurons were present in telencephalic areas that project to the OB, most notably in the posterior zone of the dorsal telencephalon (Dp).
source: Moreover, retrogradely labeled neurons were present in telencephalic areas that project to the OB, most notably in the posterior zone of the dorsal telencephalon (Dp), the homolog of mammalian olfactory cortex (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The posterior zone of the dorsal telencephalon (Dp) is the homolog of mammalian olfactory cortex.
source: Moreover, retrogradely labeled neurons were present in telencephalic areas that project to the OB, most notably in the posterior zone of the dorsal telencephalon (Dp), the homolog of mammalian olfactory cortex (Figure 1B).
evidence: Statement of established anatomical knowledge

claim: After incubation at 36 °C, substantially more neurons expressed DsRed than after incubation at 26 °C.
source: After incubation at 36 °C, substantially more neurons expressed DsRed (Figure 1B) than after incubation at 26 °C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Retrograde labeling was detected in a small but distinct population of neurons in the dorsal telencephalon at 36 °C that was not seen at 26 °C.
source: In addition, retrograde labeling was detected in a small but distinct population of neurons in the dorsal telencephalon that was not seen at 26 °C (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: DsRed expression at 36 °C was first detected ~12 hr after injection and stable for at least 10 days.
source: DsRed expression at 36 °C was first detected ~12 hr after injection and stable for at least 10 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: Similar expression was observed when the temperature was decreased from 36 °C to 26 °C 3 days after injection.
source: Similar expression was also observed when the temperature was decreased from 36 °C to 26 °C 3 days after injection, but not when it was increased from 26 °C to 36 °C after 3 days (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C

claim: Expression was not observed when temperature was increased from 26 °C to 36 °C 3 days after injection.
source: Similar expression was also observed when the temperature was decreased from 36 °C to 26 °C 3 days after injection, but not when it was increased from 26 °C to 36 °C after 3 days (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C

claim: Adjusting the temperature to that of mammalian hosts can substantially increase the efficiency of HSV1-mediated viral gene transfer in zebrafish.
source: These results show that adjusting the temperature to that of mammalian hosts can substantially increase the efficiency of HSV1-mediated viral gene transfer in zebrafish.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing gene expression at different temperatures

claim: Expression of GFP was detected at 28.5 °C after injection of HSV1[LTCMV:GFP] into the optic tectum of zebrafish larvae at 3 dpf.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Zou et al., 2014), expression of GFP was detected at 28.5 °C (N=3 fish) but the number of GFP-positive cells increased when temperature was raised to 32 °C (N=5) or 35 °C (N=10; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Zou et al., 2014

claim: The number of GFP-positive cells increased when temperature was raised to 32 °C or 35 °C after injection of HSV1[LTCMV:GFP] into the optic tectum of zebrafish larvae at 3 dpf.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Zou et al., 2014), expression of GFP was detected at 28.5 °C (N=3 fish) but the number of GFP-positive cells increased when temperature was raised to 32 °C (N=5) or 35 °C (N=10; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: Strong and widespread expression was observed when HSV1[LTCMV:GFP] was injected at 5 dpf and fish were subsequently kept at 35 °C for 48 hr.
source: Strong and widespread expression was also observed when the virus was injected at 5 dpf (N=14) or 14 dpf (N=9) and fish were subsequently kept at 35 °C for 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C

claim: Strong and widespread expression was observed when HSV1[LTCMV:GFP] was injected at 14 dpf and fish were subsequently kept at 35 °C for 48 hr.
source: Strong and widespread expression was also observed when the virus was injected at 5 dpf (N=14) or 14 dpf (N=9) and fish were subsequently kept at 35 °C for 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C

claim: When HSV1[LTCMV:GFP] was injected into muscles of the trunk at 5 dpf, strong and selective retrograde labeling of motor neurons in the spinal cord was observed after keeping fish at 35 °C for 48 hr.
source: When HSV1[LTCMV:GFP] was injected into muscles of the trunk at 5 dpf, strong and selective retrograde labeling of motor neurons in the spinal cord was observed after keeping fish at 35 °C for 48 hr (N=4; Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D

claim: HSV1 can be used for gene delivery and retrograde neuronal tracing throughout development.
source: These results indicate that HSV1 can be used for gene delivery and retrograde neuronal tracing throughout development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data at different developmental stages

claim: HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] did not drive expression when injected into the brain of wildtype zebrafish.
source: This virus did not drive expression when injected into the brain of wildtype zebrafish (N=3; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: mCherry was co-expressed with GFP in a subset of Purkinje neurons and putative Golgi cells after injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; gad1b:GFP] fish.
source: mCherry was co-expressed with GFP in a subset of Purkinje neurons and putative Golgi cells (97.7% ± 1.2% of mCherry-positive neurons were also GFP-positive; mean ± s.d.; N=4 fish; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: 97.7% ± 1.2% of mCherry-positive neurons were also GFP-positive in the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; gad1b:GFP] fish after injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry].
source: mCherry was co-expressed with GFP in a subset of Purkinje neurons and putative Golgi cells (97.7% ± 1.2% of mCherry-positive neurons were also GFP-positive; mean ± s.d.; N=4 fish; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative experimental data

claim: No expression was detected in the dense population of GFP-negative granule cells in the granular layer after injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; gad1b:GFP] fish.
source: No expression was detected in the dense population of GFP-negative granule cells in the granular layer.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: 94.8% ± 4.5% of mCherry-positive neurons coexpressed GFP after injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] near Dp in Tg[gad1b:GFP; gad1b:Gal4] fish.
source: Co-expression of mCherry and GFP was observed also when the injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] was directed at a cluster of GABAergic neurons near Dp in adult Tg[gad1b:GFP; gad1b:Gal4] fish (94.8% ± 4.5% of mCherry +neurons coexpressed GFP; mean ± s.d.; N=5 fish; Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C

claim: mCherry-expressing neurites arborized extensively in the lateral pallium but spared a region of Dp immediately adjacent to the gad1b-positive cluster.
source: Interestingly, mCherry-expressing neurites arborized extensively in the lateral pallium but spared a region of Dp immediately adjacent to the gad1b-positive cluster, indicating that the dorsal telencephalon contains specific long-range projections of GABAergic neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The dorsal telencephalon contains specific long-range projections of GABAergic neurons.
source: Interestingly, mCherry-expressing neurites arborized extensively in the lateral pallium but spared a region of Dp immediately adjacent to the gad1b-positive cluster, indicating that the dorsal telencephalon contains specific long-range projections of GABAergic neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of mCherry-expressing neurites

claim: Expression of GFP was detected selectively in DsRed-positive cells in the hindbrain and cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; gad1b:DsRed] larvae after injection of HSV1[UAS:GFP].
source: In zebrafish larvae (7 dpf), we injected HSV1[UAS:GFP] into the hindbrain of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; gad1b:DsRed] fish (N=3) and detected expression of GFP selectively in DsRed-positive cells in the hindbrain and cerebellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E

claim: HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system to enhance the specificity of cellular targeting.
source: These observations indicate that HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system to enhance the specificity of cellular targeting.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing selective expression in Gal4-expressing cells

claim: Injection of HSV1[UAS:Venus-CAAX] into the optic tectum of Tg[th:Gal4; UAS:tdTomato-CAAX] fish resulted in the selective expression of Venus-CAAX in a small number of tdTomato-CAAX-positive neurons in the locus coeruleus.
source: We first injected HSV1[UAS:Venus-CAAX] into the optic tectum of Tg[th:Gal4; UAS:tdTomato-CAAX] fish, which express Gal4 and the red-fluorescent protein tdTomato-CAAX under the control of the tyrosine hydroxylase-1 promoter, a marker for catecholaminergic neurons. This procedure resulted in the selective expression of the membrane-associated protein Venus-CAAX in a small number of tdTomato-CAAX-positive neurons in the locus coeruleus with complex long-distance axonal projections, indicating that expression was specifically directed to catecholaminergic (noradrenergic) neurons (Figure 2D; N=4 fish).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Expression of GFP was observed specifically in OB-projecting neurons of the dorsal telencephalon after injection of HSV1[LTCMV:Gal4] into the OB and HSV1[UAS:GFP] into the dorsal telencephalon.
source: In additional experiments, we first injected HSV1[LTCMV:Gal4] into the OB of wildtype zebrafish and subsequently injected HSV1[UAS:GFP] into the dorsal telencephalon. Expression of GFP was observed specifically in OB-projecting neurons of the dorsal telencephalon without expression elsewhere (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The Gal4/UAS system and the one-component approach yielded similar numbers of labeled neurons in the dorsal telencephalon.
source: To assess the efficiency of this intersectional targeting approach, we compared the number of labeled neurons using either the Gal4/UAS system or the one-component approach (injection of HSV1[LTCMV:DsRed] into OB). Both approaches yielded similar numbers of labeled neurons in the dorsal telencephalon (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2F

claim: HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system in intersectional approaches with high efficiency and low leakiness.
source: We therefore conclude that HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system in intersectional approaches with high efficiency and low leakiness.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing different targeting approaches

claim: Co-packaging of red and green reporter constructs into the same virus resulted in 89.5% ± 8.7% co-expression in the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish.
source: When red and green reporter constructs were co-packaged into the same virus (HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry & UAS:GFP]), injection into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] resulted in a high rate of co-expression, as expected (89.5% ± 8.7% co-expression; mean ± s.d.; N=3 fish; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C

claim: Co-injection of separate viruses (HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] and HSV1[UAS:GFP]) produced 84.3% ± 6.0% co-expression in the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish.
source: Interestingly, co-injection of the same responder constructs packaged into separate viruses (HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] and HSV1[UAS:GFP]) produced a similar rate of co-expression, even when overall expression was sparse (84.3% ± 6.0% co-expression; mean ± s.d.; N=3 fish; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C

claim: Co-packaging and co-injection of viruses can be used to express multiple transgenes in the same neurons.
source: These results indicate that co-packaging and co-injection of viruses can be used to express multiple transgenes in the same neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data on co-expression rates

claim: Brief (500ms) illumination with red light evoked GCaMP6f fluorescence transients that increased in amplitude with increasing light intensity in OB-projecting neurons co-expressing GCaMP6f and Chrimson-tdTomato.
source: Brief (500ms) illumination with red light evoked GCaMP6f fluorescence transients that increased in amplitude with increasing light intensity (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; 21 neurons in one fish).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Transgene-expressing neurons were functional and responsive to optogenetic stimulation.
source: Hence, transgene-expressing neurons were functional and responsive to optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from optogenetic stimulation experiments

claim: Fish injected with HSV1[UAS:TeNT-GFP] into the cerebellum showed abnormal body posture and swimming patterns.
source: To explore loss-of-function manipulations we expressed tetanus toxin light chain (TeNT) in GABAergic neurons of the cerebellum by injecting HSV1[UAS:TeNT-GFP] into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish. Injected fish showed abnormal body posture and swimming patterns such as slow swimming, circular or 'corkscrew' trajectories, and a tendency to stay in the lower portion of the water column, whereas control fish injected with HSV1[UAS:GFP] swam normally (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 2—videos 1–3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and videos

claim: Control fish injected with HSV1[UAS:GFP] into the cerebellum swam normally.
source: To explore loss-of-function manipulations we expressed tetanus toxin light chain (TeNT) in GABAergic neurons of the cerebellum by injecting HSV1[UAS:TeNT-GFP] into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish. Injected fish showed abnormal body posture and swimming patterns such as slow swimming, circular or 'corkscrew' trajectories, and a tendency to stay in the lower portion of the water column, whereas control fish injected with HSV1[UAS:GFP] swam normally (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 2—videos 1–3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and videos

claim: Virally delivered TeNT-GFP modified synaptic output of GABAergic neurons in the cerebellum.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that virally delivered TeNT-GFP modified synaptic output of GABAergic neurons in the cerebellum, although further experiments are needed to fully understand the mechanism underlying the observed effects on swimming behavior.
evidence: Hypothesis inferred from behavioral effects, but further experiments needed

claim: HSV1-mediated gene transfer offers a wide range of opportunities for anatomical and functional experiments in zebrafish.
source: HSV1-mediated gene transfer thus offers a wide range of opportunities for anatomical and functional experiments in zebrafish.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental demonstrations

claim: A collection of 26 different HSV1s for applications in zebrafish has been assembled.
source: We have so far assembled a collection of 26 different HSV1s for applications in zebrafish (Figure 2—source data 1 file1).
evidence: Supported by list in Figure 2—source data 1 file1

claim: Fifteen HSV1s drive expression of fluorescent markers, calcium indicators, Gal4 or optogenetic probes under the control of the non-specific LTCMV promoter.
source: Fifteen of these drive expression of fluorescent markers, calcium indicators, Gal4 or optogenetic probes under the control of the non-specific LTCMV promoter for regional transgene expression and retrograde tracing.
evidence: Description of the HSV1 collection

claim: Eleven HSV1s drive expression of fluorescent markers, optogenetic probes, toxins and other proteins under UAS control.
source: The remaining 11 HSV1s drive expression of fluorescent markers, optogenetic probes, toxins and other proteins under UAS control for intersectional targeting of neurons using the Gal4/UAS system.
evidence: Description of the HSV1 collection

claim: In rodents, modified rabies viruses have become important tools to analyze connectivity and structure-function relationships in neuronal circuits.
source: In rodents, modified rabies viruses have become important tools to analyze connectivity and structure-function relationships in neuronal circuits.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field

claim: Modified rabies virus vectors can infect specific 'starter' neurons and are transmitted retrogradely to presynaptic neurons across one synapse.
source: These vectors can infect specific 'starter' neurons and are transmitted retrogradely to presynaptic neurons across one synapse.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about rabies virus vectors

claim: Specific infection of rabies virus is achieved by expressing the receptor protein TVA in the starter neuron and pseudotyping the virus with the envelope protein EnvA.
source: Specific infection is achieved by expressing the receptor protein TVA in the starter neuron and pseudotyping the virus with the envelope protein EnvA (Wickersham et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wickersham et al., 2007a

claim: To limit retrograde transfer to one synapse, an essential glycoprotein (G) is deleted from the viral genome and supplied in trans only in the starter neurons.
source: To limit retrograde transfer to one synapse, an essential glycoprotein (G) is deleted from the viral genome and supplied in trans only in the starter neurons.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about rabies virus methodology

claim: The G-deleted rabies virus (RVΔG) has been reported to infect neurons in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, the G-deleted rabies virus (RVΔG) has been reported to infect neurons (Zhu et al., 2009) and to cross synapses when complemented with G but the efficiency of retrograde synaptic transfer appeared very low (Dohaku et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2009

claim: RVΔG has been reported to cross synapses when complemented with G in zebrafish, but the efficiency of retrograde synaptic transfer appeared very low.
source: In zebrafish, the G-deleted rabies virus (RVΔG) has been reported to infect neurons (Zhu et al., 2009) and to cross synapses when complemented with G but the efficiency of retrograde synaptic transfer appeared very low (Dohaku et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dohaku et al., 2019

claim: No GFP expression was observed when EnvA-RVΔG-GFP was injected into the telencephalon of wildtype fish at 36 °C.
source: When we injected EnvA-coated RVΔG expressing GFP (EnvA-RVΔG-GFP) into the telencephalon of wildtype fish at 36 °C, no GFP expression was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Efficient and selective infection of neurons expressing GFP was observed at 36 °C after injection of EnvA-RVΔG-GFP into the telencephalon of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish.
source: We then injected EnvA-RVΔG-GFP into the telencephalon of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish that express TVA-mCherry in GABAergic neurons. After 6 days, efficient and selective infection of neurons expressing GFP was observed at 36 °C but not at 26 °C, nor when the temperature was raised from 26 °C to 36 °C 3 days post injection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Infection of zebrafish neurons by EnvA-RVΔG-GFP required TVA.
source: Hence, infection of zebrafish neurons by EnvA-RVΔG-GFP required TVA and was substantially more efficient when the temperature was close to the body temperature of natural hosts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of infection in wildtype vs. TVA-expressing fish

claim: Infection of zebrafish neurons by EnvA-RVΔG-GFP was substantially more efficient when the temperature was close to the body temperature of natural hosts.
source: Hence, infection of zebrafish neurons by EnvA-RVΔG-GFP required TVA and was substantially more efficient when the temperature was close to the body temperature of natural hosts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from temperature comparison experiments

claim: Of 19,819 endogenous genes analyzed, 522 were significantly downregulated while 27 were significantly upregulated in RVΔG-infected cells.
source: Of 19,819 endogenous genes analyzed, 522 were significantly downregulated while 27 were significantly upregulated in infected cells (see Materials and methods for details on statistics).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data analysis

claim: Stress markers occurred with approximately average frequency among genes regulated in RVΔG-infected cells.
source: Among these, stress markers occurred with approximately average frequency (downregulated: 27 out of 471 stress marker genes; upregulated: 1/471) and cell death markers were underrepresented (downregulated: 14/651 genes; upregulated: 4/651; Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—source data 1 file1).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A–B

claim: Cell death markers were underrepresented among genes regulated in RVΔG-infected cells.
source: Among these, stress markers occurred with approximately average frequency (downregulated: 27 out of 471 stress marker genes; upregulated: 1/471) and cell death markers were underrepresented (downregulated: 14/651 genes; upregulated: 4/651; Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—source data 1 file1).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A–B

claim: The 65 gene ontology (GO) terms that were significantly associated with the set of regulated genes were primarily related to immune responses.
source: The 65 gene ontology (GO) terms that were significantly associated with the set of regulated genes were primarily related to immune responses while GO terms related to stress, cell death, electrophysiological properties or synapses were rare or absent (Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—source data 2 file2).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—source data 2 file2

claim: GO terms related to stress, cell death, electrophysiological properties or synapses were rare or absent among significantly associated GO terms.
source: The 65 gene ontology (GO) terms that were significantly associated with the set of regulated genes were primarily related to immune responses while GO terms related to stress, cell death, electrophysiological properties or synapses were rare or absent (Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—source data 2 file2).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—source data 2 file2

claim: The observed changes in gene expression may reflect a general immune response.
source: The observed changes in gene expression may therefore reflect a general immune response but they do not suggest major effects of RVΔG on physiological functions or cellular stress levels.
evidence: Interpretation of RNA sequencing data

claim: Changes in gene expression do not suggest major effects of RVΔG on physiological functions or cellular stress levels.
source: The observed changes in gene expression may therefore reflect a general immune response but they do not suggest major effects of RVΔG on physiological functions or cellular stress levels.
evidence: Interpretation of RNA sequencing data

claim: No obvious differences were detected in the time course or amplitude distribution of odor responses between RVΔG-infected neurons and uninfected neurons.
source: No obvious differences were detected in the time course or amplitude distribution of odor responses between infected neurons (N=1293 neurons from four fish) and uninfected neurons (N=559 from the same four fish; Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E–G

claim: Infection with RVΔG did not compromise the health or physiological function of neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate that infection with RVΔG did not compromise the health or physiological function of neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNA sequencing and calcium imaging data

claim: Efficient transneuronal spread of the rabies virus depends on the expression level of the viral glycoprotein in starter cells.
source: Efficient transneuronal spread of the rabies virus depends on the expression level of the viral glycoprotein in starter cells (Kim et al., 2016; Miyamichi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2016 and Miyamichi et al., 2013

claim: Codon usage was optimized for zebrafish to enhance glycoprotein expression.
source: We therefore took two steps to enhance glycoprotein expression. First, we optimized codon usage for zebrafish.
evidence: Description of methodological approach

claim: TVA and the codon-optimized glycoprotein (zoSADG) were expressed using HSV1 because viral vectors typically reach higher expression levels than transgenics.
source: Second, we expressed TVA and the codon-optimized glycoprotein (zoSADG) using HSV1 because viral vectors typically reach higher expression levels than transgenics (Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2014

claim: In rodents, starter neurons expressing high levels of G often disappear in parallel with the emergence of transneuronal expression, presumably because long-term expression of G is toxic.
source: In rodents, starter neurons expressing high levels of G often disappear in parallel with the emergence of transneuronal expression, presumably because long-term expression of G is toxic (Faber et al., 2002; Ohara et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Faber et al., 2002 and Ohara et al., 2013

claim: GABAergic Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum receive local synaptic input from different types of cerebellar neurons and long-range input from neurons in the contralateral inferior olive (climbing fibers).
source: We first focused on the cerebellum where GABAergic Purkinje neurons receive local synaptic input from different types of cerebellar neurons and long-range input from neurons in the contralateral inferior olive (climbing fibers; Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement of established anatomical knowledge, illustrated in Figure 4A

claim: Expression of GFP was restricted to putative starter neurons when EnvA-RVΔG-GFP and HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] were co-injected into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish in the absence of glycoprotein.
source: We first focused on the cerebellum where GABAergic Purkinje neurons receive local synaptic input from different types of cerebellar neurons and long-range input from neurons in the contralateral inferior olive (climbing fibers; Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: No expression of GFP was detected in the inferior olive when EnvA-RVΔG-GFP and HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] were co-injected into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish in the absence of glycoprotein.
source: No expression of GFP was observed in the inferior olive, consistent with the expectation that RVΔG does not spread in the absence of glycoprotein.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The number of mCherry-expressing Purkinje neurons and putative Golgi cells declined over the incubation period of 10 days when zoSADG was supplied in trans.
source: To examine whether the delivery of glycoprotein to starter cells can drive transneuronal spread, we injected a mixture of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry], HSV1[UAS:zoSADG] and EnvA-RVΔG-GFP into the cerebellum of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish. Unlike in the absence of glycoprotein, the number of mCherry-expressing Purkinje neurons and putative Golgi cells now declined over the incubation period of 10 days.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The number of neurons expressing GFP was low initially but increased steeply between 6 and 10 days after injection when zoSADG was supplied in trans.
source: The number of neurons expressing GFP, in contrast, was low initially but increased steeply between 6 and 10 days after injection (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Injecting EnvA-RVΔG-GFP 2 or 4 days after the injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] and HSV1[UAS:zoSADG] did not result in a further increase in the number of infected neurons.
source: Injecting EnvA-RVΔG-GFP 2 or 4 days after the injection of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] and HSV1[UAS:zoSADG] did not result in a further increase in the number of infected neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with observations in rodents (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Wertz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations to Vélez-Fort et al., 2014 and Wertz et al., 2015

claim: GFP was expressed in Purkinje cells and throughout the granular layer in the cerebellum when zoSADG was supplied in trans.
source: In the cerebellum, GFP was expressed in Purkinje cells and throughout the granular layer (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The number and spatial distribution of GFP-expressing neurons in the granular layer was clearly different from mCherry expression in the absence of glycoprotein, indicating that GFP was expressed in granule cells.
source: The number and spatial distribution of GFP-expressing neurons in the granular layer was clearly different from mCherry expression in the absence of glycoprotein (Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish injected with HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry]; Figure 2B), indicating that GFP was expressed in granule cells.
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 4C and Figure 2B

claim: GFP-positive neurons were found in the contralateral inferior olive when zoSADG was supplied in trans.
source: Moreover, GFP-positive neurons were found in the contralateral inferior olive (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Trans-complementation with zoSADG in starter cells promoted transneuronal spread of the rabies virus.
source: We therefore conclude that trans-complementation with zoSADG in starter cells promoted transneuronal spread of the rabies virus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing GFP expression in presynaptic neurons

claim: The convergence index for transneuronal viral transfer for synaptic inputs to Purkinje neurons from the inferior olive was 1.00±0.95.
source: The convergence index was 1.00±0.95 (mean ± s.d.; N=4 fish; Figure 4E), which is comparable to values reported in mammals (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4E and comparison to Kim et al., 2016

claim: The convergence index for transneuronal viral transfer for synaptic inputs to Purkinje neurons from the inferior olive is comparable to values reported in mammals.
source: The convergence index was 1.00±0.95 (mean ± s.d.; N=4 fish; Figure 4E), which is comparable to values reported in mammals (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison to Kim et al., 2016

claim: Both glutamatergic principal neurons and GABAergic interneurons in Dp receive long-range input from mitral cells in the OB.
source: In this area, both glutamatergic principal neurons and GABAergic interneurons receive long-range input from mitral cells in the OB (Figure 4F).
evidence: Statement of anatomical knowledge, illustrated in Figure 4F

claim: GFP expression was largely restricted to a cluster of neurons that co-expressed mCherry when HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] and EnvA-RVΔG-GFP were injected into Dp of Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish without zoSADG.
source: When a mixture of HSV1[UAS:TVA-mCherry] and EnvA-RVΔG-GFP was injected into Tg[gad1b:Gal4] fish (Figure 4G), GFP expression was largely restricted to a cluster of neurons that co-expressed mCherry (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The cluster of GFP/mCherry co-expressing neurons was located near a prominent furrow that separates an anterior from a posterior compartment of Dp, consistent with the known location of GABAergic neurons in Dp.
source: This cluster was located near a prominent furrow that separates an anterior from a posterior compartment of Dp, consistent with the known location of GABAergic neurons in Dp (Frank et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by anatomical observation and citation to Frank et al., 2019

claim: When HSV1[UAS:zoSADG] was added to the injected virus mixture in Dp, mCherry expression became rare while a large number of neurons in different telencephalic areas expressed GFP.
source: When HSV1[UAS:zoSADG] was added to the injected virus mixture, mCherry expression became rare while a large number of neurons in different telencephalic areas expressed GFP (Figure 4H1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: GFP was expressed in the olfactory bulb by neurons with the characteristic morphology of mitral cells when HSV1[UAS:zoSADG] was added to the injected virus mixture in Dp.
source: Moreover, GFP was expressed in the olfactory bulb by neurons with the characteristic morphology of mitral cells, but not by other cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: vglut1 is expressed in excitatory neurons in the telencephalon but not in the OB.
source: Note that vglut1 is expressed in excitatory neurons in the telencephalon but not in the OB (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), implying that labeling of OB neurons cannot be explained by direct infection.
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Labeling of OB neurons cannot be explained by direct infection when viruses are injected into Dp of Tg[vglut1:Gal4] fish.
source: Note that vglut1 is expressed in excitatory neurons in the telencephalon but not in the OB (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), implying that labeling of OB neurons cannot be explained by direct infection.
evidence: Inferred from vglut1 expression pattern

claim: Convergence indices for projections of mitral cells to GABAergic starter neurons in Dp was 0.70±0.21.
source: Convergence indices for projections of mitral cells to GABAergic or glutamatergic starter neurons in Dp were 0.70±0.21 and 1.31±1.20 (mean ± s.d.; N=5 and N=4 fish, respectively; Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4J

claim: Convergence indices for projections of mitral cells to glutamatergic starter neurons in Dp was 1.31±1.20.
source: Convergence indices for projections of mitral cells to GABAergic or glutamatergic starter neurons in Dp were 0.70±0.21 and 1.31±1.20 (mean ± s.d.; N=5 and N=4 fish, respectively; Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4J

claim: EnvA-RVΔG selectively infects TVA-expressing target neurons and undergoes monosynaptic retrograde transneuronal transfer when complemented with zoSADG.
source: These results confirm that EnvA-RVΔG selectively infects TVA-expressing target neurons and undergoes monosynaptic retrograde transneuronal transfer when complemented with zoSADG.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in cerebellum and telencephalon

claim: In the absence of zoSADG, GFP expression was restricted to mCherry-positive neurons around the injection site in the spinal cord of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish at 10 dpf.
source: To examine transneuronal viral spread at early developmental stages, we injected EnvA-RVΔG-GFP into the spinal cord of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish at 10 dpf and analyzed fluorescence after 6–7 days. In the absence of zoSADG, GFP expression was restricted to mCherry-positive neurons around the injection site (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: When zoSADG was supplied in trans, GFP expression was observed throughout the spinal cord and in the brainstem after injection into the spinal cord of Tg[gad1b:Gal4; UAS:TVA-mCherry] fish at 10 dpf.
source: When zoSADG was supplied in trans by co-injecting EnvA-RVΔG-GFP with HSV1[UAS:zoSADG], GFP expression was observed throughout the spinal cord and in the brainstem (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: GFP-positive neurons distant from the injection site did usually not co-express mCherry when zoSADG was supplied in trans.
source: GFP-positive neurons distant from the injection site did usually not co-express mCherry.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: Glycoprotein-dependent retrograde transneuronal transfer occurs at larval stages.
source: We therefore conclude that glycoprotein-dependent retrograde transneuronal transfer also occurs at larval stages.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in larvae

claim: Effects of temperature on the expression of virally delivered transgenes cannot easily be explained by increased proliferation of infected cells or other indirect effects.
source: Effects of temperature on the expression of virally delivered transgenes cannot easily be explained by increased proliferation of infected cells or other indirect effects.
evidence: Reasoning about potential mechanisms

claim: Temperature shift experiments suggest that temperature affects gene expression by modulating the process of viral infection.
source: Temperature shift experiments suggest that temperature affects gene expression by modulating the process of viral infection but the precise mechanism is not understood and additional effects on protein synthesis may also occur.
evidence: Interpretation of temperature shift experiments

claim: A transient temperature shift around the time of virus injection was sufficient to achieve high expression.
source: Because a transient temperature shift around the time of virus injection was sufficient to achieve high expression, fish can be returned to standard laboratory temperature days before follow-up experiments are usually performed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from temperature shift experiments

claim: Fish can be returned to standard laboratory temperature days before follow-up experiments are usually performed.
source: Because a transient temperature shift around the time of virus injection was sufficient to achieve high expression, fish can be returned to standard laboratory temperature days before follow-up experiments are usually performed.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: The temperature shift is expected to have minimal effects on subsequent experiments such as activity measurements or behavioral analyses.
source: The temperature shift is therefore expected to have minimal effects on subsequent experiments such as activity measurements or behavioral analyses.
evidence: Inference from behavioral and activity data

claim: HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system for two-component control of gene expression without obvious leakiness.
source: Our results show that HSV1 can be combined with the Gal4/UAS system for two-component control of gene expression without obvious leakiness.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Intersectional strategies are important to target narrowly defined types of neurons by combining the genetic specificity of promoters with the spatial and temporal precision of viral injections.
source: Such intersectional strategies are important to target narrowly defined types of neurons by combining the genetic specificity of promoters with the spatial and temporal precision of viral injections.
evidence: Statement of methodological principle

claim: Expression can be directed to specific neurons by injecting HSV1 with UAS-dependent inserts into existing Gal4 driver lines.
source: Importantly, expression can be directed to specific neurons by injecting HSV1 with UAS-dependent inserts into existing Gal4 driver lines.
evidence: Description of methodological approach

claim: Viral delivery of UAS responders may be useful to overcome the slow loss of expression observed in some Gal4/UAS transgenic lines over generations.
source: Conceivably, viral delivery of UAS responders may also be useful to overcome the slow loss of expression observed in some Gal4/UAS transgenic lines over generations because it bypasses epigenetic silencing of the highly repetitive UAS elements (Akitake et al., 2011; Goll et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Akitake et al., 2011 and Goll et al., 2009

claim: Viral delivery of UAS responders bypasses epigenetic silencing of the highly repetitive UAS elements.
source: Conceivably, viral delivery of UAS responders may also be useful to overcome the slow loss of expression observed in some Gal4/UAS transgenic lines over generations because it bypasses epigenetic silencing of the highly repetitive UAS elements (Akitake et al., 2011; Goll et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akitake et al., 2011 and Goll et al., 2009

claim: The HSV1 toolbox opens novel opportunities for the fast and flexible interrogation of neurons in zebrafish.
source: This toolbox opens novel opportunities for the fast and flexible interrogation of neurons in zebrafish.
evidence: Conclusion about the utility of the toolbox

claim: Temperature adjustments were important for enhanced transneuronal spread of rabies virus in zebrafish.
source: We further established procedures for retrograde monosynaptic tracing using rabies viruses that greatly enhanced the efficiency of transneuronal transfer compared to a previous study in zebrafish (Dohaku et al., 2019). Temperature adjustments were important but unlikely to be the only factor underlying the enhanced transneuronal spread because the temperature difference to the previous study was only 1.5 °C (Dohaku et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison to previous study (Dohaku et al., 2019)

claim: Temperature adjustments were unlikely to be the only factor underlying the enhanced transneuronal spread because the temperature difference to the previous study was only 1.5 °C.
source: Temperature adjustments were important but unlikely to be the only factor underlying the enhanced transneuronal spread because the temperature difference to the previous study was only 1.5 °C (Dohaku et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison to previous study (Dohaku et al., 2019)

claim: Increased glycoprotein expression by codon optimization, viral gene delivery, and possibly small differences in the experimental schedule contributed significantly to enhanced transneuronal spread.
source: We therefore assume that increased glycoprotein expression by codon optimization, viral gene delivery, and possibly small differences in the experimental schedule also contributed significantly.
evidence: Inference about factors contributing to enhanced transneuronal spread

claim: High levels of the viral glycoprotein G are toxic to cells within a few days in rodents.
source: Experiments in rodents indicate that high levels of the viral glycoprotein G are toxic to cells within a few days (Faber et al., 2002; Ohara et al., 2013) while the G-deficient Rabies virus, RVΔG, exhibits toxicity on longer timescales (>2 weeks) (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Wickersham et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Faber et al., 2002 and Ohara et al., 2013

claim: The G-deficient Rabies virus, RVΔG, exhibits toxicity on longer timescales (>2 weeks) in rodents.
source: Experiments in rodents indicate that high levels of the viral glycoprotein G are toxic to cells within a few days (Faber et al., 2002; Ohara et al., 2013) while the G-deficient Rabies virus, RVΔG, exhibits toxicity on longer timescales (>2 weeks) (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Wickersham et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chatterjee et al., 2018 and Wickersham et al., 2007b

claim: Starter neurons expressing G disappeared during the first 10 days after virus injection in zebrafish.
source: Consistent with these notions, we found that starter neurons expressing G disappeared during the first 10 days after virus injection whereas neurons infected with RVΔG in the absence of G did not substantially decline in number.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Neurons infected with RVΔG in the absence of G did not substantially decline in number in zebrafish.
source: Consistent with these notions, we found that starter neurons expressing G disappeared during the first 10 days after virus injection whereas neurons infected with RVΔG in the absence of G did not substantially decline in number.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: RVΔG primarily changed the expression of immunity-related genes in zebrafish.
source: Transcriptional profiling revealed that RVΔG primarily changed the expression of immunity-related genes, suggesting no obvious effects on cellular health or physiology on the timescales explored here.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data

claim: Transneuronally labeled neurons remain physiologically functional for up to 10 days even though starter neurons disappear.
source: It is therefore likely that transneuronally labeled neurons remain physiologically functional for up to 10 days even though starter neurons disappear.
evidence: Inference from RNA sequencing and calcium imaging data

claim: These results are consistent with observations in rodents and provide a time window for a wide range of experiments.
source: These results are consistent with observations in rodents (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Wickersham et al., 2007b; Wickersham et al., 2007a) and provide a time window for a wide range of experiments, including anatomical labeling and functional analysis of neurons connected to specific starter cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chatterjee et al., 2018, Wickersham et al., 2007b, and Wickersham et al., 2007a

claim: Transneuronal spread of rabies viruses was glycoprotein-dependent and labeled substantial numbers of putative presynaptic neurons from different starter neurons, both in adult zebrafish and in larvae.
source: Transneuronal spread of rabies viruses was glycoprotein-dependent and labeled substantial numbers of putative presynaptic neurons from different starter neurons, both in adult zebrafish and in larvae.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Convergence ratios were similar to those observed in rodents despite the fact that zebrafish neurons are smaller and probably receive fewer synaptic inputs.
source: Convergence ratios were similar to those observed in rodents despite the fact that zebrafish neurons are smaller and probably receive fewer synaptic inputs.
evidence: Comparison of convergence ratios to rodent studies

claim: The efficiency of transneuronal tracing was in the same range as in rodents.
source: These results suggest that the efficiency of transneuronal tracing was in the same range as in rodents although quantitative comparisons are difficult.
evidence: Inference from convergence ratio data

claim: Rabies-based methods for transneuronal tracing are subject to ongoing developments with the general goal to further increase efficiency and reduce toxicity.
source: Rabies-based methods for transneuronal tracing are subject to ongoing developments with the general goal to further increase efficiency and reduce toxicity (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Ciabatti et al., 2017; Ciabatti et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple recent studies

claim: Rabies-based transneuronal tracers are promising tools for the structural and functional dissection of neuronal circuitry in zebrafish.
source: Hence, rabies-based transneuronal tracers are promising tools for the structural and functional dissection of neuronal circuitry in zebrafish.
evidence: Conclusion about the utility of rabies-based tracers

claim: Retrograde tracing of connected neuronal cohorts using rabies viruses has become an important approach to decipher the functional logic of neuronal connectivity in rodents.
source: Retrograde tracing of connected neuronal cohorts using rabies viruses has become an important approach to decipher the functional logic of neuronal connectivity in rodents.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field

claim: The small size of zebrafish facilitates the combination of neuronal circuit tracing with other methods such high-resolution imaging of neuronal activity patterns throughout large brain areas.
source: The small size of zebrafish facilitates the combination of neuronal circuit tracing with other methods such high-resolution imaging of neuronal activity patterns throughout large brain areas.
evidence: Statement about advantages of zebrafish as a model system

claim: Anterograde transneuronal tracing using VSVs may complement retrograde transneuronal tracing by rabies viruses.
source: Transneuronal tracing in the anterograde direction from starter neurons that were not genetically defined has previously been achieved using VSVs in larval zebrafish (Kler et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019; Mundell et al., 2015). Hence, anterograde transneuronal tracing using VSVs may complement retrograde transneuronal tracing by rabies viruses.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kler et al., 2021, Ma et al., 2019, and Mundell et al., 2015

claim: The temporal resolution of viral gene transfer will be limited by the time required for viral gene expression (days).
source: Viral gene transfer may therefore be used also for developmental studies but the temporal resolution will be limited by the time required for viral gene expression (days).
evidence: Inference from time-course data

claim: Viral gene transfer will be most useful for the analysis of neuronal circuit structure and function in juvenile or adult fish.
source: Hence, we expect that viral gene transfer will be most useful for the analysis of neuronal circuit structure and function in juvenile or adult fish, similar to the application of viral tools for systems neuroscience in rodents.
evidence: Inference about optimal applications

claim: The ability to target gene expression to specific neurons opens new opportunities for the functional dissection of neuronal circuits in zebrafish.
source: The ability to target gene expression to specific neurons opens new opportunities for the functional dissection of neuronal circuits in zebrafish.
evidence: Conclusion about the utility of viral gene transfer

claim: Juvenile and adult zebrafish exhibit a richer repertoire of behaviors than larvae that includes social affiliation and associative learning.
source: Juvenile and adult zebrafish exhibit a richer repertoire of behaviors than larvae that includes, for example, social affiliation and associative learning (Dreosti et al., 2015; Valente et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dreosti et al., 2015 and Valente et al., 2012

claim: Transgene expression often declines at developmental stages when complex behaviors emerge in zebrafish.
source: At the developmental stages when these behaviors emerge, the use of transgenic lines for the functional dissection of neuronal circuitry becomes increasingly difficult because transgene expression often declines.
evidence: Statement of known limitation of transgenic approaches

claim: Viral gene transfer is a promising strategy to extend genetic manipulations into juvenile or adult stages.
source: Viral gene transfer is therefore a promising strategy to extend genetic manipulations into juvenile or adult stages.
evidence: Inference from limitations of transgenic approaches

claim: Some brain areas including the telencephalon remain optically accessible even at late juvenile or adult stages.
source: Some brain areas including the telencephalon remain optically accessible even at late juvenile or adult stages, allowing for optical measurements of neuronal activity during behavior (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2020

claim: Viral tools and their combination with genetic and optical approaches offer a wide range of experimental opportunities that have not been available in zebrafish so far.
source: Viral tools and their combination with genetic and optical approaches therefore offer a wide range of experimental opportunities that have not been available in zebrafish so far.
evidence: Conclusion about the impact of the developed tools
